summary: This program builds a list of Book objects for a small library, then walks through that list to collect each book's genre into a second list of strings and prints them. It shows how one collection can be used to build another.

lines.text: List is the interface that describes an ordered collection; declaring variables as List keeps your code flexible about which implementation you use.
The angle brackets say this list holds Book objects only, so the compiler catches any attempt to add something else.
Creating the object and adding it to the list are two separate steps; at this point Eragon exists but the library does not know about it yet.
add() appends the book to the end of the list, so the order of these calls is the order the books will be visited later.
A second list, this time of plain strings, ready to receive one genre per book.
The enhanced for loop hands you each Book in turn without you having to manage an index counter.
Each book is asked for its genre and that string is stored in the genres list, which is how you extract one field from a collection of objects.
The \n escape sequence prints a blank line before the heading, which separates this section visually from any earlier output.
Looping over the new list proves it was filled correctly and shows that genres repeat, since three books share the Fantasy genre.
